en.title: Father and Daughter Duo Unpack Shared Obsession with True Crime
en.summary: Acclaimed author **Lauren Oliver** and her father, **Harold Schechter**, reveal the origins of their mutual fascination with the darker aspects of human nature. Their candid conversation explores how childhood influences shaped a lifelong interest in crime writing.
en.body:
It's not every day a father and daughter share a professional passion for the grim realities of murder and mayhem. Yet, for authors **Lauren Oliver** and **Harold Schechter**, this shared obsession forms the bedrock of their latest literary exploration. Released in 2026, their joint work delves into the fascinating intersection of crime writing and familial connection, offering a unique perspective for fans of both genres.


Schechter, a renowned crime historian, traces his fascination back to a childhood steeped in classic monster movies and eerie comic books. "I spent my Friday evenings watching our local Creature Features TV programs that showed the classic Universal monster movies like Frankenstein, Dracula, and The Wolfman," he recalls. This early immersion in the fantastical soon morphed into a profound curiosity about the real-life monsters who populated the darker corners of society. "For me, that need was fulfilled by real-world murders who seemed like fairy-tale ogres come to life," Schechter explains, citing figures like Ed Gein, whose chilling story inspired iconic horror films like **The Texas Chain Saw Massacre** and **Psycho**.


Oliver, herself a bestselling author, shares this deep-seated interest, demonstrating how such obsessions can be passed down and nurtured within a family. Their dialogue, presented in their new book, goes beyond mere recounting of notorious cases; it examines the psychological and sociological roots of our fascination with crime. It’s a conversation that resonates with anyone who has ever found themselves drawn to the compelling, albeit disturbing, narratives that true crime offers, whether in fiction or non-fiction.

## A Shared Literary Landscape

This Father's Day collaboration isn't just a personal reflection; it’s a testament to the enduring power of storytelling and the complex human psyche. For readers who devour mysteries, thrillers, and true crime accounts, the opportunity to hear from two prominent voices in the field, especially when they are family, offers a rich and insightful experience. It taps into a community that thrives on dissecting motives, exploring genre evolution, and appreciating the craft behind weaving tales of suspense and intrigue. The book invites readers to consider their own relationship with dark narratives and the reasons behind our collective pull towards them.


## Exploring the Dark Side Together

The bond between **Schechter** and **Oliver** in their exploration of crime writing highlights a unique dynamic within the literary world. It provides a compelling narrative for fans who appreciate authorial backgrounds and the personal journeys that shape creative output. This conversation is particularly relevant for those interested in how genre conventions are established and how personal experiences can fuel professional endeavors. It’s a reminder that even the darkest subjects can be explored with intellectual rigor and a profound appreciation for the art of storytelling, offering insights that extend beyond the crime genre itself.


## What's Next

Fans eager to dive deeper into **Harold Schechter** and **Lauren Oliver's** shared fascination can find their book, "A Father and Daughter Discuss Their Shared Crime Obsessions," available now. Further discussions and insights into their respective writing careers are anticipated.

tr.title: Babalar Günü: Babayla Kızın Paylaştıkları Suç Obsesyonu
tr.summary: Ünlü yazar Lauren Oliver ve babası Harold Schechter, suç yazılarındaki ortak meraklarının kökenlerini ortaya koyuyor. Samimi bir sohbetle, suç yazılarına olan yaşam boyu ilgiyi şekillendiren çocukluk etkilerini keşfediyorlar. Babayla kızın paylaştıkları bu obsesyon, yeni kitaplarında suç yazımı ve aile bağlantısının ilginç kesişimini sunuyor.
tr.body:
Her gün bir baba ve kızın birlikte suç yazılarına olan profesyonel bir tutkuyu paylaşmaları nadirdir. Ancak yazar Lauren Oliver ve babası Harold Schechter için bu paylaşılan obsesyon, son literatür araştırmalarının temelini oluşturuyor. 2026'da yayınlanan ortak eserleri, suç yazımı ve aile bağlantısının benzersiz bir perspektif sunuyor.

 
   ## Paylaşılan Bir Merak
   Ünlü suç tarihçisi Harold Schechter, bu merakının kökenini klasik canavar filmleri ve korku komiklerine dayanan bir çocukluğa bağlar. "Cuma akşamları yerel Canavar Özellikleri TV programlarını izlerdim, bu programlar klasik Universal canavar filmlerini gibi Frankenstein, Drakula ve Kurt Adam'ı gösterirardi," diye hatırlıyor. Bu erken dönemde fantastik öğelerle büyümesi, toplumun daha karanlık köşelerinde yaşayan gerçek canavarlara karşı derin bir merakla sonuçlandı. "Benim için bu ihtiyaç, gerçek dünya katilleri tarafından karşılandı, bunlar adeta peri masallarındaki canavarlar gibi görünüyordu," diye açıklıyor ve Ed Gein gibi isimlere atıfta bulunuyor, bunların hikayeleri **The Texas Chain Saw Massacre** ve **Psycho** gibi ikonik korku filmlerine ilham verdi.

 
   ## Birlikte Yazın Dünyası
   Lauren Oliver, bu derin ilgiyi paylaşıyor ve böyle obsesyonların nasıl bir aile içinde geçirilebileceğini ve beslenebileceğini gösteriyor. Yeni kitaplarında sunulan diyalog, yalnızca ünlü suçların basit bir şekilde anlatımının ötesine geçerek, suçla ilgili merakımızın psikolojik ve sosyolojik köklerini inceliyor. Bu, true crime'ın sunduğu komplo dolu, ama rahatsız edici hikayelere çekilen herkesle rezonans gösteren bir konuşma.

 
   ## Karanlık Tarafı Birlikte Keşfetmek
   Bu Babalar Günü işbirliği, sadece kişisel bir yansıma değil, aynı zamanda hikaye anlatmanın kalıcı gücüne ve kompleks insan psikolojisine bir tanıklık. Suç yazıları, gerilim ve true crime hesaplarını seven okuyucular için, bu alanda iki önemli sesi, özellikle de aile bağlantısını duymanın zengin ve aydınlatıcı bir deneyimi sunuyor. Kitap, okuyucuların karanlık hikayelerle olan ilişkilerini ve bu çekiciliğin nedenlerini düşünmeye davet ediyor.

 
   ## Sonraki Adımlar
   Lauren Oliver ve Harold Schechter'in paylaştıkları suç obsesyonuna daha derine dalmak isteyen hayranlar, "Bir Baba ve Kızın Paylaştıkları Suç Obsesyonları" adlı kitabını şimdi okuyabilir. Yazarların yazı kariyerleri hakkında daha fazla tartışma ve fikir bekleniyor.

content_raw: For Father’s Day, we asked authors Lauren Oliver and Harold Schechter, who happen to be daughter and father, to have a wide-ranging conversation about writing and crime. Happy reading! Lauren Oliver: It’s rare for a father and daughter to share a professional obsession with the darkest corners of the human psyche. I’d love to start with how you first found your way into writing about murder and crime. Harold Schechter: I’ve been asked that many times, and the answer always goes back to my childhood fascination with monsters. As a baby boomer, I grew up in a culture saturated with them. I spent my Friday evenings watching our local Creature Features TV programs that showed the classic Universal monster movies like Frankenstein , Dracula , and The Wolfman . I went to Saturday matinees of Grade-B horror films like Creature from the Black Lagoon and The Incredible Shrinking Man . I pored over comics like Tales from the Crypt and magazines like Famous Monsters of Filmland . My imagination was shaped—if not warped—by those stories. As I grew older, I became fascinated by the psychological and sociological function these stories serve—why do we need tales about monsters from childhood on? At a certain age, you stop believing in werewolves, but you never outgrow the need for a substitute. For me, that need was fulfilled by real-world murders who seemed like fairy-tale ogres come to life. LO: Like Ed Gein? HS: Exactly. While researching a book on movie special effects, I realized that The Texas Chain Saw Massacre and Psycho, my all-time favorites horror films, were both inspired by the midwestern “ghoul,” Ed Gein. Looking into his case—which most people, me included, were unfamiliar with at the time—I was struck by the fact that it was a kind of nightmarish folktale come to life. It’s a universal experience: every community has a story about the “creepy character” living off the beaten track—the Boo Radley types. Those figures invariably turn out to be harmless eccentrics. In the Bronx apartment building I grew up in, there was an old woman on the sixth floor we whispered was a cannibal witch. Of course, she turned out to be nothing but a lonely old cat lady. But in Gein’s case, the stories about his “haunted house” were actually true. When I wrote my early books, I didn’t even think of them as true crime. I felt I was inventing a new genre: “true horror.” LO: It’s interesting you say that, because I grew up in a house saturated with those real-life monsters. When I started writing my first thriller, it felt like a homecoming. I’ve always been interested in the “shadow”—the Jungian idea that these monsters are just the embodiment of dark impulses that are present, in a refracted way, in regular people. HS: Precisely. Monsters are the incarnations of our forbidden, antisocial impulses. They’re manifestations of what Jung called the shadow archetype. LO: But there was a weird duality for me.
